sources.text:
A Data / ML Engineering Bootcamp at VAST Data in 2025, as an internship. The team built a smart agriculture system. Sarah built two components of it entirely on her own: weed detection, and image embeddings with similarity search.

- An end-to-end weed detection pipeline with Python, PyTorch and MobileNetV3: fetching images from MinIO, running inference, and storing the results in PostgreSQL.
- An image embedding system with CLIP / ViT-mini, publishing vectors to Kafka and loading them into pgvector for similarity search and analytics.
- Containerizing backend and AI services in Docker, for reproducible development and deployment.

- `weed-detection-pipeline`: weed detection on CPU with MobileNetV3, after UNet proved impractical without a GPU.
- `clip-embeddings-kafka`: image embeddings with CLIP / ViT-mini, through Kafka into pgvector, with similarity search on request.

AI Engineer at Ainsof Capital in 2026, working remotely. Sarah was the sole engineer of a production data-governance platform, and owned it end to end, from architecture design through launch.

The platform manages reliable information. Every piece of information has a source, a trust score, and a full record of who changed what and when. When two sources contradict each other, the system detects it and sends it to a person to check, instead of deciding on its own.

The product and its business domain are not described here.

- Designing the claims-based data model: every fact is sourced, trust-scored, auditable and checked for conflicts.
- Building the PostgreSQL layer: schemas, migrations, row-level security, triggers, RPC functions, optimistic concurrency and idempotency keys.
- Building the governance API that the data center works against.
- Performance work on the API.
- Building a machine translation pipeline on the Claude API, behind a human approval gate.
- Building the 28-screen governance center and the bilingual, offline-first travel PWA.

A separate team built the scraping that pulls data from websites, which is one of the sources of claims.

- `claims-trust-model`: the claims-based data model, with trust, conflicts and human review.
- `postgres-rls-backbone`: the PostgreSQL layer, with three schemas, row-level security and safe concurrent writes.
- `api-latency-582-to-40`: cutting API latency from 582ms to 40ms per request.
- `human-gated-translation`: machine translation with the Claude API that never overwrites a person's edit.
- `governance-center-pwa`: the 28-screen governance center and the bilingual offline-first PWA.

A Data / ML Engineering Bootcamp at VAST Data in 2025, as an internship. The team built a smart agriculture system. Sarah built two components of it entirely on her own: weed detection, and image embeddings with similarity search.

- An end-to-end weed detection pipeline with Python, PyTorch and MobileNetV3: fetching images from MinIO, running inference, and storing the results in PostgreSQL.
- An image embedding system with CLIP / ViT-mini, publishing vectors to Kafka and loading them into pgvector for similarity search and analytics.
- Containerizing backend and AI services in Docker, for reproducible development and deployment.

- `clip-embeddings-kafka`: image embeddings with CLIP / ViT-mini, through Kafka into pgvector, with similarity search on request.

A CV compresses years of work into a few lines that nobody can verify. "Built a RAG system" looks the same from someone who shipped one and someone who followed a tutorial, and most of Sarah's best work was done for employers, so it has no public link. This agent is one link where anyone can ask what matters to them about her experience, get an answer grounded in cited sources, and inspect the engineering behind it: the sources, the quality numbers, the decisions and the code.

- **Every claim must come from a source.** The agent may only say what the knowledge base says, and cite it, so retrieval quality is the product, not a detail.
- **Hebrew and English.** Most visitors ask in Hebrew, while the records are written in English. Plain keyword search fails across languages.
- **Zero cost, public traffic.** Only free tiers, and no free service whose terms forbid a public app (ADR-0009 rules out the free Gemini tier on the visitor path). Groq quotas cap how many experiments can run in a day.
- **Numbers, not impressions.** Every design choice is decided by a rule written before the experiment runs, on a labeled dataset, with confidence intervals.

Sarah owns the product, the specification and every decision: she wrote and approved the spec chapter by chapter, labeled the evaluation sets, and approved each ADR before it was accepted. She built the system with Claude Code as her coding partner, which is why the commits carry a Claude co-author line.

The knowledge base is a folder of Markdown records (`portfolio/`) with a strict frontmatter schema, checked in CI by a Pydantic validator, plus a publication check that blocks banned terms in any tracked file. Records are ingested into Neon Postgres, one chunk per record (C4), with `tsvector`, trigram and pgvector indexes. Postgres has no Hebrew dictionary, so text is normalized the same way at ingestion and at query time: final letters become regular letters, and niqqud and cantillation marks are removed. Embedding models run in process with ONNX Runtime (quantized, CPU).

The FastAPI agent streams answers over SSE. To search, it writes its own English query (Q1) through the `search_portfolio` tool; code strips Sarah's name from that query, because the name pulled generic records to the top. Retrieval is hybrid (R3): a lexical ranking (BM25 and trigrams, fused with RRF) and a vector ranking (multilingual-e5-small, cosine) fused again with RRF, k = 60. Each hit keeps its lexical, vector and fused scores so the trace panel can show why it was chosen. The LLM runs on Groq.

The UI is Next.js with Hebrew (RTL) and English routes, deployed with the backend in one Vercel project (ADR-0004).

Quality is measured on four datasets: D1 (96 retrieval questions with gold chunks, split dev/test, test never read), D2 (36 adversarial cases), D3 (11 job ads with labeled requirements, including injection attempts) and D4 (12 multi-turn conversations). Database tests run against PGlite in CI.

**Chunking: one chunk per record (C4).** Rejected: a chunk per heading (C1), with or without a context header (C2), and grouped sections (C3). Why: C4 had the highest Recall@5 (0.76 vs 0.46 for C1), significantly better than all three, and the records are small enough to fit (ADR-0010).

**Hybrid retrieval (R3).** Rejected: lexical only (R1) and vectors only (R2). Why: R1 and e5 missed different questions, and fusing them reached 0.88, significantly better than either alone (ADR-0011).

**multilingual-e5-small for embeddings.** Rejected: e5-base and bge-m3 (no better, and slower: bge-m3 ~800 ms per query), MiniLM and Qwen3 (weaker), and Gemini (best on quality, 0.90, but its free tier is not allowed on the visitor path). Why: as good as the larger models in R3, and the smallest and simplest (ADR-0012).

**The agent writes the query, and code strips the name (Q1).** The first Q1 run scored worse than the raw question (0.78 vs 0.88), because the model added "Sarah Halevy" to 36 of 50 queries and that pulled the FAQ record to the top. Sarah chose to keep Q1 and strip the name in code, which brought it to 0.87 (ADR-0013).

The first reranking run reported a median of 16.5 seconds per call, far too slow for a chat. The number was wrong, not the model: Groq's rate limit answered with 429, the client waited and retried, and the timer counted the waiting as part of the call. The fix was to record the wait separately from the call time. Measured that way, the real rerank call takes 1.5 seconds at the median and 1.9 at p95 (31 calls). Latency is now reported without rate-limit waits, and the waits are counted on their own.

On the D1 dev split, hybrid retrieval with one chunk per record finds the right sources in the top 5 for 0.88 of the labeled sources (Hebrew 0.86, cross-lingual 0.91). LLM reranking (R4) is under evaluation: its first run scored significantly higher, and by the stopping rule written before the run, two more runs decide whether it is adopted. The agent loop, the UI and the hardening are still being built (milestones M4-M6), and this record is updated as each one lands.

sources.text:
AI Engineer at Ainsof Capital in 2026, working remotely. Sarah was the sole engineer of a production data-governance platform, and owned it end to end, from architecture design through launch.

The platform manages reliable information. Every piece of information has a source, a trust score, and a full record of who changed what and when. When two sources contradict each other, the system detects it and sends it to a person to check, instead of deciding on its own.

The product and its business domain are not described here.

- Designing the claims-based data model: every fact is sourced, trust-scored, auditable and checked for conflicts.
- Building the PostgreSQL layer: schemas, migrations, row-level security, triggers, RPC functions, optimistic concurrency and idempotency keys.
- Building the governance API that the data center works against.
- Performance work on the API.
- Building a machine translation pipeline on the Claude API, behind a human approval gate.
- Building the 28-screen governance center and the bilingual, offline-first travel PWA.

A separate team built the scraping that pulls data from websites, which is one of the sources of claims.

- `claims-trust-model`: the claims-based data model, with trust, conflicts and human review.
- `postgres-rls-backbone`: the PostgreSQL layer, with three schemas, row-level security and safe concurrent writes.
- `api-latency-582-to-40`: cutting API latency from 582ms to 40ms per request.
- `human-gated-translation`: machine translation with the Claude API that never overwrites a person's edit.
- `governance-center-pwa`: the 28-screen governance center and the bilingual offline-first PWA.

A Data / ML Engineering Bootcamp at VAST Data in 2025, as an internship. The team built a smart agriculture system. Sarah built two components of it entirely on her own: weed detection, and image embeddings with similarity search.

- An end-to-end weed detection pipeline with Python, PyTorch and MobileNetV3: fetching images from MinIO, running inference, and storing the results in PostgreSQL.
- An image embedding system with CLIP / ViT-mini, publishing vectors to Kafka and loading them into pgvector for similarity search and analytics.
- Containerizing backend and AI services in Docker, for reproducible development and deployment.

- `weed-detection-pipeline`: weed detection on CPU with MobileNetV3, after UNet proved impractical without a GPU.
- `clip-embeddings-kafka`: image embeddings with CLIP / ViT-mini, through Kafka into pgvector, with similarity search on request.

sources.text:
AI Engineer at Ainsof Capital in 2026, working remotely. Sarah was the sole engineer of a production data-governance platform, and owned it end to end, from architecture design through launch.

The platform manages reliable information. Every piece of information has a source, a trust score, and a full record of who changed what and when. When two sources contradict each other, the system detects it and sends it to a person to check, instead of deciding on its own.

The product and its business domain are not described here.

- Designing the claims-based data model: every fact is sourced, trust-scored, auditable and checked for conflicts.
- Building the PostgreSQL layer: schemas, migrations, row-level security, triggers, RPC functions, optimistic concurrency and idempotency keys.
- Building the governance API that the data center works against.
- Performance work on the API.
- Building a machine translation pipeline on the Claude API, behind a human approval gate.
- Building the 28-screen governance center and the bilingual, offline-first travel PWA.

A separate team built the scraping that pulls data from websites, which is one of the sources of claims.

- `claims-trust-model`: the claims-based data model, with trust, conflicts and human review.
- `postgres-rls-backbone`: the PostgreSQL layer, with three schemas, row-level security and safe concurrent writes.
- `api-latency-582-to-40`: cutting API latency from 582ms to 40ms per request.
- `human-gated-translation`: machine translation with the Claude API that never overwrites a person's edit.
- `governance-center-pwa`: the 28-screen governance center and the bilingual offline-first PWA.

sources.text:
One PostgreSQL database served three different audiences: the public site, the internal data center where editors review and approve data, and the ingestion of data from sources. Each needed different access, and public visitors could never reach internal data. Several editors could work on the same data at the same time, and a request could fail halfway and be sent again.

The product and its business domain are not described here.

Permissions had to be enforced in the database itself, not only in application code. At the same time, editors working in parallel must not silently overwrite each other, and a retried request must not be applied twice.

Sarah designed and built the database layer end to end: the schemas, all migrations, the RLS policies, the triggers, the RPC functions, and the governance API in front of it.

**Three schemas, separated by permission:** `public` for the site, `admin` for the data center, and `ingestion` for incoming data.

**Row-level security:** the public catalog is readable by anyone; admin tables are reachable only with the service role; personal data is limited to its owner through `auth.uid()`.

**Controlled public writes:** visitors never write to tables directly. Writes such as submitting a suggestion or a report go through `SECURITY DEFINER` RPC functions, and they arrive in the data center as drafts.

**Triggers:** an automatic audit trail on every table, automatic opening of a conflict when a contradicting claim arrives, and enforcement of the per-field rules in the field catalog.

**Safe concurrent writes:** every write carries `expected_version`, like `UPDATE ... WHERE version = expected`. A stale version returns 409; the client re-reads and retries quietly, so two editors do not overwrite each other. Idempotency keys stop a request that failed halfway and was sent again from being applied twice.

**Closing the database:** in July, direct database access was closed at the infrastructure level, and the data center moved to work only through the governance API.

Auth is Supabase Auth (magic link and OAuth), with JWTs verified locally against JWKS.

**Closing direct database access, everything through the API.** Rejected: keeping direct access for the data center alongside the API. Why: one entry point means one place where permissions, versions and idempotency are enforced.

**Permissions in the database, with three schemas.** Access is separated at the database level, not only in application code.

**Public writes through `SECURITY DEFINER` RPCs.** Public writes are controlled: an RPC accepts a fixed shape and lands it as a draft.

**Optimistic concurrency with versions, plus idempotency keys.** Two editors do not overwrite each other, and a retried request is not applied twice.

The database layer is live in production. The data center works only through the governance API, editors working in parallel do not overwrite each other, and a retried request is not applied twice. Usage numbers are not shared.

sources.text:
Identify plants in an image, classify their species, and analyze their health, end to end, with inference fast enough to serve over an API.

Sarah built the whole system on her own.

An end-to-end computer vision pipeline: YOLO detects the plants, and CLIP classifies them and analyzes their health. A GPU-accelerated FastAPI backend serves the pipeline, optimized for low-latency inference, and the system is deployed on AWS EC2.

Only an overview of this project is recorded. For details beyond it, ask Sarah directly.

The system was built end to end and deployed on an AWS EC2 GPU instance.

The weed detector answers one fixed question about an image. This part turns each whole image into an embedding vector instead, so the system can ask open questions: how similar two images are, whether this is the same disease or the same phenomenon, and whether an image deviates from a set of normal ones.

Finding similar images had to be fast, without reprocessing the original images or reloading the model for every query.

The team built a whole smart agriculture system. Sarah built this part, image embeddings and similarity search, entirely on her own, as one component of that system.

An embedding model that captures visual similarity, CLIP / ViT-mini, turns each image into a vector of hundreds of numbers. The vectors are published to Kafka and loaded into PostgreSQL with pgvector.

When a new image arrives, the only automatic step is computing its vector and storing it. Similarity search runs only on request, from a user, another service, or the QA system: it takes an image's vector and compares it with the stored vectors to find the most similar images.

There are no folders or categories in pgvector. Similar images sit close to each other in the vector space, so groups form on their own, without a manual split.

**Compute each embedding once and store it.** Rejected: computing embeddings at query time. Why: a stored vector lets search run without touching the original images or reloading the model.

**Separate ingestion from query.** Rejected: running a similarity search automatically for every incoming image. Why: ingestion stays a single cheap step, and search runs only when someone needs it.

**Vectors instead of another classifier.** A classifier answers one fixed question. Vectors work on any image and allow similarity, clustering, and spotting anomalies and recurring problems.

Every incoming image gets a vector once, and any image can then be compared with the whole collection on request. Together with the weed detector, the system can both tell what is in an image and how close it is to known cases. Sarah presented it in a demo.

תורת היחסות היא מסגרת פיזיקלית שפותחה על ידי אלברט איינשטיין בתחילת המאה ה‑20, והיא מתארת כיצד המרחב והזמן מתנהגים בתנאים של מהירויות גבוהות או שדות כבידה חזקים.  

* **תורת היחסות המיוחדת** (1905) קובעת שהמהירות של האור בריק קבועה לכל צופה, ושחוקי הפיזיקה הם זהים בכל מערכת אינרציאלית. כתוצאה מכך, זמן ומרחב אינם מוחלטים אלא תלויים במהירות של הצופה – תופעות כמו התארכות זמן (time dilation) והכיווץ של אורך (length contraction).  

* **תורת היחסות הכללית** (1915) מרחיבה את הרעיון לשדות כבידה, ומתארת את הכבידה כעקמומיות של מרחב‑זמן שנגרמת על‑ידי מסה ואנרגיה. המשוואות של איינשטיין מקשרות בין תכונות של מרחב‑זמן (המתמטיקה של טנסורים) לבין תכולת החומר‑אנרגיה שבו.  

בקיצור, תורת היחסות משנה את ההבנה הקלאסית של זמן, מרחב וכבידה, ומסבירה תופעות שמדידות מדעיות מדויקות מצביעות עליהן, כגון קפיצות של לוויינים סביב כדור הארץ והפרשי זמן בין שעונים על פני כדור הארץ ובחלל.
